Then somebody asked whether we could try the last verse again. Somebody else found a second harmony, and suddenly we had three opinions about where to breathe. None of them seemed wrong. We packed our folders and sang the final chord out on the steps, where it sounded much better than it had any right to. A couple of people walking past stopped and waited until we finished. Every autumn I announce that this will be the year I label the boxes before putting them in the attic. Every spring I bring down a box marked "misc" and discover four scarves, a cracked flowerpot, and the instruction book for a fan I no longer own. I then promise myself that I will sort everything before it goes back upstairs. The promise usually lasts until I have to carry the box. This year I bought proper labels. They are still in their wrapper on the kitchen table, where I pass them several times a day.

My sister says the labels need a home of their own before they can help anything else. She is annoyingly right. She also suggested that I make a list of the boxes on my phone, which sounds sensible until I picture myself in the attic trying to work out which of three boxes called "winter things" I meant. I have already made one such list. It is titled "attic maybe" and contains the single word "lights".

To be fair to me, the attic is not an inviting place. The bulb works only when it feels like it, and the ladder has to come out of the shed first. Last time I went up, I found the missing wooden chess piece we blamed on the dog. I brought it down and then put it somewhere so safe that I cannot now find it. The dog, who is no longer with us, deserves an apology whenever it turns up again.

I could call this a lesson about organization, but mostly it is a story about how long I can avoid a ladder. If the rain stops on Sunday, I may finally go up there. Perhaps I will take the labels with me. Perhaps I will spend the afternoon finding the ladder and call that progress. Please don't ask me on Monday how it went.

On the first Friday of each month, we set out a long table in the hall and ask anyone nearby to bring something they have been making. Last time there were knitted mittens, a nearly finished model boat, and a folder of family recipes. The owner of the boat was still deciding how to attach its little mast, and three people offered different ideas. Nobody solved it on the spot, but it was good to see people make room for a question that small and spend time thinking about it together.

You do not have to have a finished piece or know how to explain it. Some people bring the thing they are working on; others bring a photo because the real thing will not fit through the door. Sometimes people just want to see what others are doing. We have had quiet evenings and noisy ones, and both have been good. If you are curious but unsure whether your project counts, it probably does. We have never needed a rule about that.

The next table is this Friday from 5 to 7. Come for a few minutes if that is all you have. We will have tea and a spare corner for projects that need space. Children are welcome with an adult, and it is fine to arrive empty-handed. You can take a seat, look around, and leave whenever you need to. There is no presentation or sign-up sheet, only the table and the people who happen to be there that evening.

A few regulars asked whether they should bring supplies for everyone. That is kind, but there is no need. If you have scraps you were going to throw away and think somebody could use, bring them; otherwise, bring yourself. I hope to see a few familiar faces and some new ones too. The hall can be hard to spot from the road, so follow the path beside the noticeboard and look for the open side door.

data.text:
Archived guides: internal FAQ

**Why does the archive keep old copies of guides?**
The archive keeps a copy of every published guide so readers can follow older links. When a guide changes, its old address points to the archived version rather than the latest one.

**Is that a bug?**
No, it's intentional. A link in a training document should continue to show the instructions that were current when that document was written. People comparing an old procedure with today's procedure need to know which version they are reading, especially when the steps look nearly the same at first glance.

**How can I tell I'm on an archived page?**
An archived page has a date below its title and cannot be edited.

**How do I find the current guide?**
Use the blue Current version link at the top of the archived page. It takes readers out of the archive and into the guide they should use now.

**What if there's no Current version link?**
The link is absent when a guide has been withdrawn without a replacement. In that case, the archived page is a record of what was published, not an invitation to keep following those instructions. If you're answering a question, check whether a current version exists before you share an archive link as advice.

**The current guide is missing content. Where do I report it?**
Report the problem from the current page. Reports sent from the archive are routed to a different queue, because they refer to a preserved version. Starting from the page with the problem helps the receiving team see which version needs attention. You can't edit an archived copy to repair the current guide, even if the missing content is visible in that older copy.

**Is the archive a backup for drafts?**
No. It is not a way to recover an unpublished draft. Drafts are stored separately and may be deleted under the normal retention policy. The archive only holds guides that were published at least once. A draft that was never published will not appear there, no matter how complete it was when someone last worked on it.

data.text:
Red light in the first minute after you connect the scanner
Your scanner may show a red light during its first minute after you connect it. During that first check, the light means it is checking the paper path. It does not, by itself, mean there is a jam.
- Leave the sheet out while the check runs.
- Wait for the light to turn white before loading paper.
- If the light stays red for more than two minutes, turn the scanner off, clear any paper from the slot, and start it again.

Keep this first-minute light separate from a red light that appears while a sheet is moving.

Red light after a sheet enters
If the light turns red only after a sheet enters, look at where the paper stopped.
1. Remove the sheet by pulling it gently in the direction it was moving. Do not pull it backward through the rollers.
2. After the sheet comes out, check for torn paper before trying another sheet. A scrap left in the path can make the next attempt look like the same problem, so inspect the slot rather than feeding a new sheet immediately.

If the red light repeats
If the red light repeats after you have cleared the path and tried another sheet, a worn roller may be involved. Support can help confirm that possibility from a short video of the feed. The video shows how the sheet moves just before the light changes; a still photo of the red light alone does not show that behavior. A repeated light is a reason to ask for help. It is not enough information on its own to say a roller definitely needs replacing.

Sending a video to support
There is no need to send a video of the documents you were trying to scan. A blank sheet is enough to show the feed behavior.
- Before recording, remove any paper with private information from the area in view.
- Show the scanner taking in a sheet and, if it happens again, the point where it stops.
- Keep private information out of the video you send to support.

I used to think the quiet part of a meeting meant nobody had an idea. At the archive, people often need a minute to look at the photograph before they talk about it. The first time I helped lead a session, I kept jumping in with background details because I worried the silence meant I had lost everyone. A colleague let the pause run, and then someone pointed out a detail in the window that none of us had noticed.

Now I try not to fill every pause. It doesn't always work; when I'm nervous, I still start explaining too soon. But I've learned that waiting can be part of listening. Sometimes people are finding the words, and sometimes they just need another moment with the picture. I still have to remind myself that a quiet room isn't necessarily an empty one.

I was sure the old footbridge would be the thing I missed most. It was, for a while. I knew how it sounded when the boards were damp, and I could tell from the light whether the river was running high. Then I noticed I missed knowing which window in the bakery would be open after five, and who would be sitting on the bench even when it was cold. Those details weren't important on their own, but they made the walk feel familiar.

The new place is good. The bus is easier, and I can walk to the market without checking the route first. I just haven't learned its small landmarks yet, which is different from feeling at home. I think I expected that feeling to arrive all at once, like unpacking the last box. Instead, I'm slowly collecting names and routines. Maybe one day I'll know which shop window stays lit late, or recognize the person on the corner bench. For now, I still look for the footbridge in my head when I take the long way home.
